angle: Reps got jealous of enterprise deals, emailed 40 people at one company in a week, and killed deliverability
post_first_line: 40 people at one company. One week.
linkedin_post:
40 people at one company. One week.

That's what quietly tanked a team's deliverability.

A couple of reps on one team saw the ticket price on enterprise deals and got very excited. Jealous, honestly, of the reps working those accounts.

So they started sending to 40 different people at the same large company in the same week.

We had two cohorts, mid-market and enterprise. Prior data showed things going well. Then behavior changed, and enterprise recipients stopped receiving emails at the same rate.

The dashboard told us something broke. It didn't tell us why.

We had to inspect the actual sequences and look at what changed from a sending perspective. That's where we found it: certain sending behaviors were driving the deliverability problem.

Big deal sizes make reps do irrational things. Nobody was being malicious. They were chasing the bigger payout.

If you only watch the aggregate numbers, you'll miss this. You have to go look at the sends.

Have your reps ever over-blasted one account?
carousel: Slide 1: 40 people at one company in a single week
Slide 2: Reps saw enterprise ticket sizes and got jealous
Slide 3: Enterprise recipients stopped receiving emails at the same rate
Slide 4: Prior data looked healthy, so the cause wasn't obvious
Slide 5: We had to inspect the actual sequences that went out
Slide 6: Certain sending behaviors were driving the deliverability problem
Slide 7: Big deal sizes change rep behavior, so watch the sends
Slide 8: Aggregate metrics tell you something broke, not why

lesson.title: When Enterprise Envy Wrecks Deliverability
takeaways: Large deal sizes can push reps to over-send to one account, and that hurts deliverability.
A cohort-level drop tells you something changed but not what. You have to inspect the actual sequences.
Compare against prior history when things were going well to pinpoint the moment behavior shifted.
lesson.exercise: Pull last week's sends for your enterprise accounts and count how many people each rep emailed per company. Flag any account with a spike compared to your normal pattern.

angle: If your only email variable is first name, you have work to do.
post_first_line: 10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.
linkedin_post:
10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.

Most teams think they've solved it with one variable.

Copy variation matters for deliverability. You don't want to send the same email thousands of times across your recipients.

So I always recommend templated variables. First name, and the mailboxes you're sending from.

The mailboxes should feed into sequences with copy that uses spin tax or is uniquely generated.

Variation beats static every time. Variables are the easy path to adding some degree of it.

But here's my caveat: if your only variable is the recipient's first name, you have work to do.

First name is the floor, not the strategy.

What variables are you using beyond first name?
carousel: Slide 1: 10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.
Slide 2: Copy variation protects your deliverability. Static copy at scale doesn't.
Slide 3: Use templated variables in every send, without exception.
Slide 4: Variables should cover first name and the sending mailbox.
Slide 5: Link mailboxes to sequences with spin tax or uniquely generated copy.
Slide 6: Variation beats static. Variables are the easy way in.
Slide 7: If first name is your only variable, you have work to do.

lesson.title: First Name Isn't Personalization, It's the Floor
takeaways: Sending thousands of identical emails hurts deliverability, so copy variation matters.
Templated variables like first name and sending mailbox are an easy path to variation.
Pair variables with sequences using spin tax or uniquely generated copy.
lesson.exercise: Open your live sequence and count the variables. If first name is the only one, add at least one more source of variation, such as spin tax in the opening line, before your next send.

caption: First name isn't enough

angle: Who should own what when your cold email program starts slipping
post_first_line: Four teams. One cold email program.
linkedin_post:
Four teams. One cold email program.

Most programs slip because nobody knows which team owns which piece.

Here's the split I'd use.

Sales owns the sending plan. That means how many emails go out, and at the rep level, how you ramp people up to full volume.

RevOps owns list quality. Make sure the people you're sending to have legitimate mailboxes. When replies drop, RevOps can inspect which segments are actually taking the hit.

IT owns domain setup. Are your domains authenticated properly and set up to send? IT is also the team that can answer the question: what changed?

Then there's the sending vendor. Someone has to check who is sending from which domains and whether those domains are healthy. That could be RevOps, or deliverability if you have it in-house.

When replies fall off, you don't want four teams guessing. You want each team checking its own piece.

Who owns domain health on your team today?
carousel: Slide 1: Cold email slipping? Start by asking who owns what.
Slide 2: Sales owns the sending plan and volume.
Slide 3: Sales also owns rep-level ramp to full volume.
Slide 4: RevOps owns list quality and legitimate mailboxes.
Slide 5: When replies drop, RevOps inspects which segments are affected.
Slide 6: IT owns domain setup and authentication.
Slide 7: IT also answers the question: what changed?
Slide 8: Someone must own sending vendor and domain health.

lesson.title: Assign owners before cold email performance drops
takeaways: Sales owns the sending plan: total volume and how reps ramp to full volume.
RevOps owns list quality and can inspect which segments are seeing reply drops.
IT owns domain setup and authentication, and can help answer what changed; someone must also monitor sending vendor and domain health.
lesson.exercise: Write a four-row table: sending plan, list quality, domain setup, sending vendor health. Put one named owner next to each, then share it with those teams this week.

angle: New mailbox, reply rates tanked. You probably started sending too soon.
linkedin_post:
New mailbox. Reply rates tanked.

The cause is probably simpler than you think.

Maybe you just started sending too soon. That can be the whole finding.

The fix is to modify your daily sending volume. I know people have pipeline targets. This is getting deliverability granular, but the mailbox quality probably didn't match the aspirational target of your sending.

So warm the mailboxes further. Ramp your actual sends more slowly.

Then adjust from there.

It's a quick change, and it beats rewriting copy or blaming the list when the real issue is the mailbox.

What's your ramp schedule for new mailboxes?
carousel: Slide 1: New mailbox, reply rates tanked. Check this first.
Slide 2: Maybe you just started sending too soon.
Slide 3: That can be the finding. Not the copy, not the list.
Slide 4: The fix: modify your daily sending volume.
Slide 5: Pipeline targets are real. Mailbox quality still sets the ceiling.
Slide 6: Your sending target outran what the mailbox could handle.
Slide 7: Warm the mailboxes further. Ramp sends more slowly.
Slide 8: Then adjust from there.

lesson.title: When reply rates tank on a new mailbox, slow down
takeaways: Sending too soon is a valid finding when a new mailbox underperforms.
Mailbox quality needs to match the aspirational target of your sending.
The quick fix is more warming and a slower ramp of daily sends.
lesson.exercise: Pull the daily send volume for your newest mailbox. Cut it back, extend warming, and ramp up gradually while you watch reply rates.

angle: 3 things to do this week to find out why your replies dropped
linkedin_post:
3 things to do this week.

Replies dropped and nobody knows why? Start here.

First, pull up one email, or a couple. Check how many faux pas are in there. Count the links. Look at how much of the copy adds zero value.

Second, run one split test against an existing sequence. Take your lead list, split it in half, and test one change against the other.

Third, decide who owns the investigation when a drop happens. Name one person.

The drop alone won't tell you the full story. You have to see what changed at the same time as the drop.

Most teams skip that last part. They see the number fall and start guessing.

Who owns reply drops on your team?
carousel: Slide 1: Replies dropped? Do these 3 things this week.
Slide 2: First, review one email, or a couple, honestly.
Slide 3: Count the links and the faux pas in the copy.
Slide 4: Flag any copy that adds no value for the reader.
Slide 5: Second, split test against an existing sequence.
Slide 6: Split your lead list in half and test one change.
Slide 7: Third, name one owner for every drop investigation.
Slide 8: A drop alone doesn't tell you what changed.

lesson.title: How to investigate a drop in email replies
takeaways: Review a few emails for faux pas, too many links, and copy that adds little value.
Run one split test on an existing sequence by splitting your lead list in half.
Assign a clear owner for investigating drops, because the drop alone doesn't explain what changed.
lesson.exercise: Pick one live sequence this week. Count the links and flag low-value lines in one email, split the lead list in half to test one change, and write down who owns the investigation the next time replies drop.

angle: Same 10,000 emails, 36 meetings vs 28: what inbox placement costs you
linkedin_post:
10,000 emails. 36 meetings or 28.

The only thing that changed was where the emails landed.

Take two teams sending the exact same volume. One gets about 90% of its emails into the inbox and primary tab. The other gets fewer to the recipient's inbox in the first place.

Based on some reply rate assumptions, the first team turns 10,000 sends into 36 meetings. The second turns them into 28.

That's a gap of 8 meetings, and it's an illustrative example. Same list, same copy, same effort.

Depending on your price point, that gap could be hundreds of thousands of ARR that never converts into deals.

Fewer emails in the inbox means fewer meetings and less revenue. Most teams only look at reply rate and never ask how many emails actually arrived.

When did you last check your inbox placement?
carousel: Slide 1: Same 10,000 emails. 36 meetings versus 28.
Slide 2: The only variable that changed was inbox placement.
Slide 3: Team one reaches the inbox and primary tab about 90% of the time.
Slide 4: Team two reaches fewer inboxes, so fewer people ever see the email.
Slide 5: The result is a gap of 8 meetings from identical effort.
Slide 6: At the right price point, that's hundreds of thousands in ARR.
Slide 7: Fewer emails in the inbox means less revenue.
Slide 8: Check placement before you rewrite your copy.

lesson.title: Inbox placement is a revenue lever
takeaways: Holding volume, copy, and reply rate constant, placement alone moved 10,000 emails from 36 meetings to 28.
An 8-meeting delta can mean hundreds of thousands of ARR, depending on your price point.
Fewer emails reaching the inbox and primary tab means fewer meetings and less revenue.
lesson.exercise: Take your last 10,000 sends and estimate what share reached the inbox. Then multiply your reply-to-meeting rates by a 10-point lower placement rate and price the meeting gap in ARR.
